title: Authoritarian states are trying to rewire the global order – Australia and the liberal world should stop them
gist: Nick Bisley argues authoritarian cooperation has become real, routinised and well resourced — North Korea has sent more than 12,000 troops to Russia since 2024 with 30,000 more reportedly planned, China is now the second-largest contributor to the UN regular budget, and the SCO now spans 40% of world population and over 60% of the Eurasian landmass. But the coalition is thin, with divergent interests and no accepted leader, and his prescription is that Australia and like-minded states repair liberal institutions and harden supply chains, critical infrastructure and internet governance to fracture the illiberal order before it entrenches.

themes.theme: Military alignment hardening into treaty structure

insights.claim: North Korea has deployed more than 12,000 troops to fight alongside Russia's forces in Ukraine since 2024, and Zelenskyy warns during his recent Washington trip that Pyongyang is preparing to send 30,000 more.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: A 2.5x escalation in third-party manpower would materially extend Russia's war-fighting endurance — a variable for any Ukraine-conflict-duration assumption.
insights.quote: Since 2024, North Korea has deployed more than 12,000 troops to fight alongside Russia's forces in Ukraine.

insights.claim: Authoritarian military alignments have become increasingly formalised, with Russia and China signing a partnership in February 2022 just before the invasion of Ukraine and Russia and North Korea signing a security treaty in 2024.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: Formal treaties raise the cost of defection and make the alignment more durable than transactional cooperation — treat these as structural, not episodic.
insights.quote: Russia and China inked a partnership (Opens in new window) in February 2022, just prior to Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine, while Russia and North Korea signed a security treaty (Opens in new window) in 2024.
insights.locator: These alignments have become increasingly formalised

insights.claim: The Russia–China agreement fundamentally shifts the geostrategic setting in Asia, with the 2022 joint statement reading as something of an Atlantic Charter for an illiberal age — a declaration of ordering principles rather than a transactional pact.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: Reading the 2022 statement as a charter rather than a communiqué implies a long-horizon programme — the reference document for anticipating joint Sino-Russian positioning.
insights.quote: The 2022 joint statement reads as something of an Atlantic Charter for an illiberal age

insights.claim: China has been steadily advancing its influence at the UN, now the second-largest contributor to the UN regular budget and with its nationals placed in key leadership bodies across the UN system.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: Budget share plus personnel placement is how standards and norms shift quietly — watch UN technical agencies where rules on technology and data get written.
insights.quote: it is now the second-largest contributor to the UN regular budget
insights.locator: China has been steadily advancing its influence at the UN

insights.claim: The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation has expanded to include Iran, Belarus, India and Pakistan and now comprises 40 per cent of the world's population and more than 60 per cent of the Eurasian landmass, with six ASEAN members plus the ASEAN Secretary General sending leaders to the 2025 summit.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: ASEAN leader-level attendance at the SCO is the underappreciated datapoint — Southeast Asian hedging now extends to the alternative institutional architecture itself.
insights.quote: the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation has expanded to include Iran, Belarus, India and Pakistan, and now comprises 40 per cent of the world’s population and more than 60 per cent of the Eurasian landmass

insights.claim: The sclerosis of many North Atlantic institutions is what allows illiberal powers to build new bodies serving states that feel underserved by the old ones, and America's inward lurch energises the effort.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: Identifies the supply-side cause — institutional decay in the West, not just authoritarian ambition — so reform of existing bodies is the lever, not just containment.
insights.quote: The sclerosis of many North Atlantic institutions allows them to build new bodies that better serve states that feel underserved by the old ones.
insights.locator: Illiberal powers have also learned to advance

themes.theme: Contesting concepts and the information space

insights.claim: Illiberal states do not try to replace core concepts like human rights and democracy but hollow them out and refill them with authoritarian-aligned content, seeking to create a world made safe for authoritarianism.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: Semantic capture is harder to detect than open rejection — monitor definitional shifts in multilateral texts rather than headline vetoes.
insights.quote: Rather than trying to replace these terms, they seek to hollow them out and fill them with concepts aligned with illiberal interests to create a world made safe for authoritarianism.
insights.locator: Rather than trying to replace these terms

insights.claim: Authoritarian states run structured information-space coordination, bringing editors, producers and media managers to Beijing and Moscow to learn and coordinate information assaults, and pushing ideas through forums such as Hungary's Danube Club, Russia's Valdai Club and China's Xiangshan Forum.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: Names the specific institutional venues where illiberal narrative coordination happens — concrete observation points rather than abstract 'disinformation'.
insights.quote: attacking democratic systems and sharing techniques through programs that bring editors, producers and media managers to Beijing and Moscow to learn and coordinate their information assaults

themes.theme: Coalition fragility as the exploitable seam

insights.claim: The illiberal movement remains partial — there is not yet a coherent global bloc, foundations of cooperation are weak, interests and values are diverse and diverging, and there is no accepted global leader.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: Pushes back on maximalist 'axis' framing — the coalition should be modelled as loosely coupled and shockable, not monolithic.
insights.quote: There is not yet a coherent global bloc.
insights.locator: Entrepreneurial and creative as they have been

insights.claim: Despite fragility, cooperation among illiberal states is real, routinised, multidimensional and increasingly well resourced, and their ideas have strong appeal amid a rising global tide of illiberalism.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: Routinisation is the key marker — recurring institutional contact makes the alignment persistent through leadership change, raising the long-run geopolitical risk premium.
insights.quote: But cooperation among illiberal states is real, routinised, multidimensional and increasingly well resourced.
insights.locator: But cooperation among illiberal states is real

insights.claim: The turbulence of the current period is not merely a product of Sino-American competition or Russian revanchism but of coordinated efforts to recast the ideas and institutions on which the global system operates.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: Reframes geopolitical risk as institutional rather than bilateral — implies volatility persists even if US–China tensions ease.
insights.quote: The turbulence of the current period is not just the product of Sino-American competition or Russian revanchism.
insights.locator: As a country whose interests and values

insights.claim: Australia is not taking the authoritarian-cooperation threat seriously enough and must act with others to address long-term challenges to the order on which it depends.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: A named policy gap from a Lowy Institute analysis author — a precursor argument for future Australian strategic policy and defence-adjacent spending.
insights.quote: Australia is not taking this threat seriously enough.
insights.locator: Australia is not taking this threat seriously enough

insights.claim: Canberra must work with others to repair the institutional setting whose shortcomings gave authoritarians the opportunity to build alternatives, rather than only countering the alternatives themselves.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: Signals where Australian diplomatic capital should flow — multilateral reform agendas rather than new exclusive minilaterals.
insights.quote: Canberra must work with others to repair the institutional setting whose shortcomings gave authoritarians the opportunity to build alternatives.
insights.locator: What can be done beyond recognising

insights.claim: Australia should build collaborative networks to harden the social and economic infrastructure of open societies, naming supply chain resilience, critical infrastructure, internet governance standards and social cohesion as the four areas needing shoring up.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: Four named spending and regulatory priorities — supply chain resilience, critical infrastructure protection and internet governance are the sectors likely to attract Australian policy support.
insights.quote: Supply chain resilience, critical infrastructure, internet governance standards and social cohesion all need shoring up.
insights.locator: Australia should also develop collaborative networks

insights.claim: The strategic recommendation is to apply pressure to the cracks in thin illiberal coalitions to fracture the rising illiberal order before it becomes better organised and entrenched — a time-limited window.
insights.speaker: Nick Bisley
insights.so_what: Frames the next few years as the decision window; policy inaction now implies a materially harder and costlier contest later.
insights.quote: Australia and like-minded countries should apply pressure to those cracks to fracture the rising illiberal order before it becomes better organised and entrenched.
insights.locator: Illiberal states are working together to upend
